note: The third terrace of Purgatory, where anger is purged. Dante walked into its smoke at the end of Canto 15. The smoke fits the sin: anger blinds the mind and chokes it, so the souls who gave way to it now walk unseeing.

context: Dante must hold on to him like a blind man. Read as allegory, reason is the only guide through the blindness of anger.

note: Latin for "Lamb of God", a prayer sung at Mass: "Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us", ending "grant us peace". The lamb, the gentlest of animals, is Christ (John 1:29). The angry pray to the model of meekness.
Anger sets people against each other. Its cure is to sing as one, in the same words and the same measure.
Sin as a knot that ties the soul down. The penance of each terrace loosens it.
Dante's Italian says "by calends", the Roman name for the first day of each month. Only the living divide time into months. The soul has heard Dante ask a question no dead person would ask.
The body, pictured as the swaddling bands wrapped around a newborn. Dante is telling the soul that he is still alive.
The Italian says "outside modern custom": no one in recent ages has made this journey alive. In Inferno 2, Dante names the two who went before him, Aeneas and Saint Paul.

context: He speaks from inside the smoke and is never seen. Dante gives him the central speech of the poem, on free will and the ruin of the world.

note: No one aims at virtue any more. An archer unstrings his bow when he has stopped shooting.

In Canto 14, on the terrace of envy, Guido del Duca mourned the decay of Tuscany and Romagna. Marco now says the same of the whole world. Two witnesses have turned Dante's question into an urgent one: why?
Astrology. Medieval science held that the stars and planets shaped events on earth and people's characters. The question is whether they also decide how people act.
The blindness of the smoke, now said of the living. This is Canto 50 of the poem's 100, and the speech that begins here stands at its center.
The argument the whole poem rests on. If the stars forced our actions, no one could deserve Hell or Heaven, and the three realms Dante is walking through would be unjust.
Marco grants the stars a real influence. The usual medieval view was that they incline a person's temperament and first urges, but do not compel the will.

quote: a greater force and better nature
note: God. In Dante's theology each human mind is created directly by God, not by nature or the stars, so the heavens have no power over it. To be subject to God is what makes the soul free of everything else.

One of the poem's best-loved images. The newborn soul is innocent and knows only one thing: coming from a joyful God, it runs toward whatever delights it. Sin begins not in a bad nature but in a love that nobody guides.
The emperor. In Dante's political thought, set out in his treatise Monarchia, one universal ruler is needed to keep justice and peace so that people can live well.

quote: the tower of the true city
note: The true city is the City of God, the heavenly goal. A ruler need not be a saint, but he must at least see its tower from afar: he must know justice, the part of it visible from earth.
The pope. In 1300 this was Boniface VIII, whom Dante attacks throughout the poem, but the charge is against the papacy of his age as a whole.

quote: can chew the cud but doesn't split the hoof
note: The law of Moses allowed the Jews to eat only animals that both chew the cud and have a cloven hoof (Leviticus 11). Commentators read chewing the cud as meditating on Scripture. The split hoof is usually read as keeping two things apart: spiritual power and worldly power. The pope knows doctrine but grabs at both.
Worldly goods: wealth and power. The flock copies its shepherd.

quote: not that your nature is depraved
note: Marco's answer to Dante's question. Neither the stars nor a corrupt human nature is to blame. People are led badly.

The pope and the emperor. Papal writers called the pope the sun and the emperor the moon, shining only with borrowed light. Dante makes them two suns: each holds his authority directly from God, one to guide souls to Heaven, the other to guide life on earth.

quote: the sword is joined to the shepherd's staff
note: The sword is the emperor's power, the staff the bishop's crook. The popes have claimed worldly rule as well as spiritual, and with both in one hand there is no one left to check either.

quote: each plant is known by its seed
note: An echo of the Gospel saying that a tree is known by its fruit (Luke 6:44). Judge the joining of the two powers by what it has produced.

quote: the land watered by Po and Adige
note: Northern Italy: Lombardy and the region around Verona, Padua and Treviso. It was Marco's own country.

context: His long war with the popes was fought largely in northern Italy. Marco dates the region's decline from it.

quote: who has the shame to avoid
note: Bitter irony. A man too ashamed to face honest people can now cross the region in comfort, because he will not meet any.
Corrado da Palazzo, a nobleman of Brescia who served as a governor in several Italian cities, including Florence in 1276.
Gherardo da Camino, lord of Treviso from 1283 until his death in 1306, known for his generosity to poets. Dante also praises him in his Convivio as an example of true nobility.
Guido da Castello of Reggio Emilia, famous for his hospitality. He was still alive in 1300, and Dante praises him in the Convivio as well.

quote: in the French style, the honest Lombard
note: The French called all Italians "Lombards", and the word carried a bad name there, since so many Italians in France were moneylenders. Dante's word is "simple", meaning without guile. Guido was the Lombard one could trust.
Marco's conclusion, and Dante's own lifelong conviction: the Church's grab for worldly power has ruined both the Church and the world it was meant to guide.

The Levites, the priestly tribe of Israel. When the Promised Land was divided among the tribes, they alone received no territory and lived on offerings (Numbers 18). Dante takes the lesson that priests should own nothing.
Marco knows Dante's region by his speech, as souls do throughout the poem. Gherardo was so well known in Tuscany that Marco can't believe a Tuscan has not heard of him.

Gaia da Camino, who died in 1311. The early commentators disagree about her: some say she was known for her virtue, others for her loose living. If the second, the line is a last jab at how the new age has fallen from the old.
Not daybreak: it is late afternoon. Dante's word means a whitening glow, the light at the edge of the smoke, where the angel of this terrace stands.
Marco's penance is not finished, so he may not step out of the smoke into the angel's sight. He turns back before the light can show him.
